Lesson 9 · Evaluate the action

Regression adjustment and matching

Lesson 8 reconstructed why these stores adopted alerts and compared broad delivery-time groups. We now use their measured starting conditions to estimate the gain for the whole voluntary cohort.

Business question → General theory → Worked application → Synthesis

First learn the definitions, notation, and logic of the method. Then use the shared case to work through the calculation and its interpretation.

Read here or present the same material, one step at a time.

The motivating question

Managers chose whether to adopt replenishment alerts. How much did alerts help, once we account for their different starting conditions? Learn two ways to construct the missing comparison: predict both options for each store, or find comparable stores operating without alerts. Then trace both methods through the same records.

Define the experiment the observed comparison should emulate

General theory

An observational evaluation begins with the experiment we would like to run

  • Specify eligible units, treatment and usual operations
  • Set the assignment date and outcome window
  • Choose whose average effect matters
  • Explain how the observed assignment differs from random allocation

A target trial is a precise description of the experiment that would answer the decision question. It fixes eligibility, treatment strategies, time zero, follow-up, outcome and effect target before choosing an estimator. A controlled experiment assigns treatment deliberately; a natural experiment uses an external assignment event whose credibility must be argued. Voluntary adoption needs a comparison justified by recorded starting conditions.

Comparable starting conditions connect observed outcomes to the causal question

(Y(0),Y(1))⟂D∣X;0<P(D=1∣X=x)<1mj(x)=E[Y∣D=j,X=x]

D is treatment and X is the chosen set of pre-treatment controls. Conditional exchangeability says assignment carries no further information about potential outcomes once X is held fixed. Consistency relates the observed outcome to the defined treatment, and overlap supplies both options at relevant profiles. Lesson 8 develops the graph argument. Here we turn its adjustment set into estimated conditional means, m₀ and m₁.

Assignment history determines controls before any regression is fitted

  • Common causes can make adoption endogenous
  • Earlier outcomes can influence later adoption
  • Treatment-induced effort belongs inside the total effect
  • Internal validity and transfer to other populations are separate questions

Endogeneity here means that an unadjusted assignment comparison mixes treatment with other outcome determinants. Reverse causation should be dated explicitly: earlier performance can affect adoption, which then affects later performance. A time-indexed account avoids a circular graph. Use the causal story to select controls; a small p-value cannot decide which variables belong. Internal validity concerns the effect for the study population, while external validity concerns its relevance elsewhere.

Predict both potential outcomes for the same target rows

General theory

Regression adjustment predicts two outcomes for each target unit

Fit m^0(x),m^1(x) using observed outcomesτ^i=m^1(xi)−m^0(xi);ATE^=1n∑iτ^i

Fit a conditional outcome relationship using each unit’s observed treatment and outcome. Then hold its baseline characteristics fixed and predict under treatment zero and one. Only one outcome was observed for that unit; both model predictions are estimates, not newly observed counterfactuals. Averaging the paired differences standardizes to the distribution of X in the target rows.

Treatment interactions let the effect vary across starting profiles

m^(D,X)=β^0+β^DD+β^XX+γ^DXτ^(x)=β^D+γ^x

A model without treatment interactions imposes the same additive treatment contrast at every profile. Adding interactions between D and selected baseline variables allows that contrast to vary. Interacting two controls with each other can make the baseline outcome surface more flexible, but does not itself create treatment-effect heterogeneity. Specification should express the comparison and effect structure being estimated.

The population weights turn individual contrasts into ATE or ATT

All averages use the same fitted response surfaces
TargetRows averagedQuestion
ATEAll eligible unitsWhat is the average effect here?
ATTTreated unitsHow much did participants gain?
ATUUntreated unitsWhat could nonparticipants gain?

ATE, ATT and ATU are average treatment effects for all units, treated units and untreated units. Change the rows over which predictions are averaged, not the definition of a unit’s contrast. With heterogeneous effects the targets differ. A regression coefficient at one reference profile need not equal any of these population averages.

Connect the foundations before calculating

General theory

A propensity score is a conditional treatment probability

e(X)=P(D=1∣X);odds=e1−elogit(e)=log(e1−e)

The conditioning bar has the same meaning as in Lesson 2: among units with these pre-treatment inputs, what share would receive treatment? Here the binary outcome is adoption, not stockouts. A logistic model maps a linear score η to e=1/(1+exp(−η)), keeping the fitted probability between zero and one. It models the assignment process and does not by itself justify the no-unmeasured-confounding assumption.

Log odds translate a linear score into a bounded probability

The lesson fits a regularized logistic model on standardized pre-adoption inputs
Linear score ηOdds exp(η)Probability
010.50
log(3)≈1.09930.75
−log(3)≈−1.0991/30.25

Three-to-one odds means three treated for each untreated unit, hence probability 3/(3+1)=.75. C=1 is the specified inverse penalty-strength setting in the implementation; it is not a 100% probability. The matching caliper uses the logit scale and the original score SD. A well-predicted treatment label does not guarantee balance or useful overlap; inspect those outcomes of the design directly.

Construct the comparison before reading its outcome

General theory

Matching uses comparable untreated units to supply the missing comparison

For treated i, choose controls using Xτ^i=Yi−∑jwijYj,∑jwij=1Average over the retained treated units

Weights describe which untreated observations supply a treated unit’s comparison. An exact cell may use the mean of several controls; nearest-neighbor matching may use one. Choose matches from baseline variables before examining outcome differences. The resulting average targets the retained treated population, which may exclude treated units with no suitable comparison.

Exact, coarsened and distance matching define similarity differently

The matching rule determines retained units and weights
MethodHow a comparison qualifies
ExactSame values of selected baseline variables
Coarsened exactSame prespecified categories or bands
Nearest neighborSmallest distance on scaled variables
Propensity scoreNearby estimated probability of adoption

Exact matching becomes sparse as the number of distinct profiles grows. Coarsening trades finer comparability for more populated cells. A distance rule permits approximate matches but needs a scale and a policy for poor candidates. A propensity score summarizes assignment probabilities; equal estimated scores do not guarantee that a particular small matched sample balances every variable.

A caliper limits distance while replacement permits control reuse

  • Caliper: reject a candidate beyond a chosen distance
  • With replacement: a control can serve several treated units
  • Without replacement: earlier choices restrict later options
  • Record exclusions, repeated controls and the tie rule

A nearest control can still be far away, so proximity needs to be judged rather than assumed. Replacement can preserve closer comparisons but concentrates weight on a smaller number of distinct controls. The same control’s outcome is then used more than once. Tie-breaking and matching order should be explicit so another analyst can reproduce the design.

Balance evaluates the constructed comparison on the original covariates

Standardized mean difference=treated mean−weighted control meanoriginal pooled SD

Hold the original pooled within-group standard deviation fixed so the before and after numbers use the same scale. Values near zero indicate similar means; the sign shows which group is higher. Inspect distributions and overlap as well as means. Outcome prediction accuracy and assignment classification accuracy do not replace balance diagnostics.

Build the store-level analysis table

Worked application

Four hundred dated records become fifty independent store outcomes

Stores S051–S100; no stores are dropped in this release
Preparation stepRows or unitsPurpose
Voluntary cohort, weeks 17–24400 store-weeksOne common follow-up window
Average eight weeks within each store50 storesOne outcome per decision unit
Join starting conditions by store ID50 complete rowsOne-to-one merge
Split by observed adoption26 adopters; 24 controlsDefine the observed groups

Each store contributes eight post-period observations. Their mean is the outcome for this analysis, so the regression has fifty observations rather than four hundred independent store-weeks. The outcome remains a stockout percentage. The supplied lab checks eight weeks per store, a unique merge, complete inputs and the treatment count. Each week has the same monitoring exposure, making the mean of weekly rates appropriate here.

The analysis fixes adoption at week seventeen and controls measured earlier

One row per store; starting variables are measured before adoption
FieldDefinition
D1 for adoption; 0 for usual operations
YMean stockout percentage, weeks 17–24
LDelivery lead time in days
UUrban indicator: 1 urban, 0 otherwise
BBaseline stockout percentage, weeks 1–8

The measured adjustment set is delivery time, urban location and baseline performance, as established in Lesson 8. Post-alert review effort and escalations are not added to this total-effect comparison. Coding D as a binary indicator, checking its counts and recording exclusions are part of the estimand: they determine which units and options are compared. Unordered categories would use indicators with named reference levels rather than arbitrary integer scores.

S051 and S052 operated without alerts, while S053 and S054 adopted them. Baseline is measured before the choice, and outcome after it. The table lets us trace a complete row through the model and matching rules. It also distinguishes an observed post-period rate from the fitted predictions that follow.

Calculate the two fitted outcomes and their difference

Worked application

A positive reduction reverses the signed stockout effect

Signed effect=alert rate−usual-operation rateReported reduction=usual-operation rate−alert rate

General theory uses treatment minus control. In this application fewer stockouts are better, so every displayed improvement is the negative of the signed treatment effect. Rates are percentages and differences are percentage points. Keep that convention for the regression, matched pairs and cost calculation.

The fitted model separates usual operations from the alert adjustment

m^(D,L,U,B)=m^0(L,U,B)+Da^(L,U)m^0=7.110+1.137(L−3.5)+1.707U+0.296Ba^=−3.188−0.957(L−3.5)−0.294U

Least squares fits all seven coefficients jointly on the fifty observed rows. Centering delivery time at 3.5 makes the treatment coefficient refer to a nonurban store with that lead time. The baseline-rate slope is common across treatment states in this specification. The appendix gives more digits, the design matrix and the exact reproducible code. Rounded coefficients here are for reading; calculations use full precision.

S051 has an estimated usual-operation stockout rate of 11.658 percent

S051: L=3, U=1, B=11.517857m^0=7.110133+1.137155(−0.5)+1.707366+0.295988(11.517857)=11.658070%

Use the starting variables from S051’s actual row and set D=0. This is the fitted conditional mean, not its observed outcome of 12.678571%. Residual variation explains why a fitted value and observed value need not agree. Keeping that distinction clear prevents a predicted counterfactual from being presented as a measured result.

Turning alerts on changes S051’s prediction by minus 3.004 points

a^=−3.188210−0.956853(−0.5)−0.294452=−3.004235 pointsm^1=11.658070−3.004235=8.653835%Reduction=11.658070−8.653835=3.004235

Set D=1 and change both D interactions with it. Delivery time, location and baseline performance stay fixed. The baseline term cancels in this paired difference because this model contains no D×B interaction; that cancellation is a specification choice, not a general property of baseline adjustment. S051 was a control store, so its alert outcome is unobserved.

Same five starting profiles; both options predicted for each

Average the contrasts and quantify their uncertainty

Worked application

All fifty stores average a 3.01-point predicted reduction

Average usual prediction=11.22195%Average alert prediction=8.21332%Average paired reduction=11.22195−8.21332=3.00864 points

The difference of the two target averages equals the average of the fifty paired differences. Every store has weight 1/50. This standardized estimate uses delivery time, location and baseline performance together, extending Lesson 8’s broader delivery-group demonstration.

Adopter weighting raises the model’s average reduction to 3.38 points

Same fitted model; different target weights; percentage points
Target populationStoresModel reduction
All stores503.01
Adopters263.38
Nonadopters242.60

Adopters include more profiles with larger predicted benefits. The all-store estimate is the weighted average of the adopter and nonadopter estimates: (26/50)×3.38356+(24/50)×2.60247=3.00864. A management question about current adopters should use their target, while expansion to current nonadopters has a different population.

The interval uses uncertainty in the average model contrast

SE=0.31489 points95% interval=3.00864±1.96×0.31489=[2.39145,3.62583] points

The paired predictions share estimated coefficients and are therefore correlated. Averaging individual standard errors is incorrect. Average the contrast vectors first, then use the coefficient covariance matrix. This interval uses HC1 heteroskedasticity-robust covariance, a normal multiplier and the observed target covariates held fixed. Its sampling uncertainty is distinct from the substantive assignment assumptions.

Richer adjustment changes the estimate while preserving the analysis rows

All specifications use the same fifty stores
SpecificationReduction95% interval
Unadjusted2.061.00 to 3.13
Starting conditions2.902.21 to 3.60
Heterogeneous, standardized3.012.39 to 3.63

The raw comparison gives 2.06 points. A common additive treatment contrast after controlling starting variables gives 2.90. Allowing delivery and urban interactions and standardizing to all fifty stores gives 3.01. These are transparent specification changes on fixed rows. Choose controls and effect structure from the comparison argument, rather than selecting whichever estimate is largest.

Follow one adopter through a distance-based match

Worked application

Scaling makes delivery days and baseline percentages comparable in a distance

d2(i,j)=∑k(Xik−Xjksk)2s=(1.020 days, 0.496 urban, 2.458 baseline points)

Use full-cohort standard deviations with divisor n, not n−1, for this distance rule. A large numerical baseline percentage should not dominate merely because it has different units from an urban indicator. The squared Euclidean distance is a similarity rule, not a probability or a causal test. This example uses matching with replacement and no distance caliper.

S053’s closest candidate is S052 under the stated distance rule

S053: lead 5 days, urban 1, baseline 17.50%; four closest controls
CandidateLUBaseline %Distance²
S0524113.843.180
S0934113.753.289
S0653113.486.517

S053 is the first adopter in store-ID order. Compare it with every one of the 24 controls before sorting. S052 has lead time 4, urban indicator 1 and baseline rate 13.839286. Its distance is ((5−4)/1.020000)²+((1−1)/0.496387)²+((17.5−13.839286)/2.457759)²=3.179637. Outcomes play no role in choosing this candidate.

Only after selecting S052 do we calculate the observed pair difference

S052 usual-operation outcome=14.37500%S053 alert outcome=10.44643%Matched reduction=14.37500−10.44643=3.92857 points

This pair uses two different stores’ observed outcomes. It therefore differs from the regression’s two fitted outcomes for a single profile. S052 is the nearest available control under the chosen rule, not an identical store. The baseline differences remain visible in the candidate table.

Use cells to make eligibility and exclusions visible

Worked application

Exact matching on delivery and location retains twenty adopters

Selected exact cells, including both excluded profiles; all cells are in the lab
Delivery daysUrbanAdoptersControlsUse cell?
2035Yes

Within each lead-time and urban cell, average control outcomes and compare each adopter with that mean. Cells lacking either group cannot supply an observed within-cell contrast. Across all cells, 20 of 26 adopters remain and six are excluded. Exactness applies to these two variables only: baseline stockout rates can still differ within a cell.

Each retained adopter receives the mean of its exact-cell controls

Delivery 3 days, urban 1: 7 adopters and 4 controlsControl-cell mean=11.51786%S054 reduction=11.51786−8.30357=3.21429 points

Every adopter in the cell uses the same control mean, but keeps its own observed alert outcome. Pool the resulting adopter-level differences across eligible cells. Giving each cell equal weight would answer a different question because cell sizes differ. The full exact-cell estimate is 2.56205 points for the retained twenty adopters.

Adding five-point baseline bands leaves thirteen comparable adopters

Baseline band=⌊B5⌋;band 2: 10%≤B<15%Match on delivery, urban status and baseline bandRetained=1326 adopters;reduction=2.79567 points

The bands are defined before reading outcome differences. This coarsened exact match adds baseline comparability to the previous two variables, so fewer cells contain both treatment groups. For example, baseline 11.517857% belongs to band 2 and 17.5% to band 3. The reduction refers to thirteen retained adopters, not automatically all twenty-six. Closer grouping and wider population coverage are competing design considerations.

Inspect what the fitted assignment score actually achieves

Worked application

The propensity model predicts adoption from the three starting variables

e(X)=P(D=1∣X)Fit logistic adoption on standardized L,U,BMatch on logit(e^)=log(e^1−e^)

This is a model of adoption, not of the stockout outcome. The supplied implementation standardizes inputs and fits regularized logistic regression with C=1. The true propensity score has a balancing property; a fitted score and finite matching procedure still need their balance checked. Genuine absence of an untreated comparison at a relevant profile cannot be repaired by compressing variables into a score.

The logit caliper retains nineteen adopters using ten distinct controls

Caliper=0.2SD(logit(e^))=0.17333Keep nearest candidate only if distance≤caliper19 adopters retained; 7 excluded; 10 unique controls

For each adopter, choose the closest control logit with replacement. Among distances tied within 10⁻⁸, use the lowest store ID. This declared tolerance keeps the comparison stable when reading the rounded CSV exports. The caliper uses the sample standard deviation over all fifty logits. Inspect the original variables before interpreting the outcome difference; nineteen accepted pairs do not by themselves establish comparability.

Propensity matching improves delivery balance but worsens urban balance

SMD: standardized mean difference; closer to zero means closer means
Starting variableBefore SMDAfter SMD
Delivery time0.880.00
Urban indicator-0.09-0.52
Baseline stockout rate0.64-0.24

Delivery imbalance falls from 0.88 to zero. Baseline imbalance improves in magnitude from 0.64 to −0.24, but urban imbalance worsens from −0.09 to −0.52. The sign reversal tells us that the weighted controls now include a larger urban share. The design improves some dimensions while making another materially less comparable.

Eleven urban adopters face sixteen urban control appearances

Matched adopter urban share=1119=57.9%Weighted control urban share=1619=84.2%Difference=−26.3 points;SMD=−0.52

There are ten unique controls but nineteen control appearances. Counting each distinct control only once would describe a different comparison from the estimator. Urban location matters to the outcome and to the modeled alert benefit, so this substantial mismatch cannot be dismissed merely because delivery time balances.

The failed balance check calls for a revised comparison before a causal conclusion

  • Keep the 3.54-point result as a diagnosis of this attempted match
  • Try exact urban matching before ranking candidates within urban groups
  • Review baseline balance, distances and lost adopters again
  • Judge the design before reopening outcome differences

The worked redesign later in this lesson implements exact urban status plus the same logit caliper. Before reading its result, predict which adopters might be lost and which balance checks must be repeated. Exact urban matching removes urban mean imbalance for retained pairs, but can lose adopters or worsen another covariate. Another option is to reconsider nonlinear terms in the assignment model using baseline balance. Freeze a defensible comparison rule and disclose its retained target before estimating and reporting the outcome contrast.

Compare methods for identical target populations

Worked application

Comparing the same retained adopters separates method differences from population changes

Percentage points; propensity result fails the displayed urban balance check
Matching ruleAdoptersMatched reductionModel on same adopters
Nearest covariates262.903.38
Exact L and U202.562.97
Plus baseline bands132.803.06
Propensity caliper193.543.03

The model is fitted once on all fifty stores; only its averaging rows change. For the nineteen propensity-retained adopters, its average is 3.03134 points, compared with the matching attempt’s 3.54323. Comparing the latter directly with the 3.38356 model average for all twenty-six adopters would mix a method change with a population change. Agreement alone would not prove identification, and disagreement should trigger inspection of the constructed comparisons.

The spending question uses the effect for the stores covered by the decision

Value per point=140×0.01×6=8.4 CU/weekAll-store model saving=8.4×3.00864−20=5.27 CU/store-week

The stated accounting scenario charges 20 currency units per week for alerts and values each avoided stockout product-day at 6. The all-store model estimate implies a positive average saving, with uncertainty inherited from the effect estimate. Continuing current adopters and extending to nonadopters use their respective target averages. Carry this observational evidence alongside the randomized pilot, with its population and design stated.

Work through the reasoning gap

Worked application

Exact location matching retains eighteen adopters under the original logit caliper

Same estimated scores and caliper; candidates must now share urban status
Frozen redesign ruleObserved result
Exact urban status; original logit caliper0.17
Retained / excluded adopters18 / 8
Unique controls / maximum reuse10 / 3

Choose this redesign in response to the urban-balance failure, using inputs and treatment labels only. Loop through adopters in store-ID order, find the closest eligible control, apply the unchanged caliper, and permit reuse. Freeze the accepted pairs before merging outcomes. The retained adopters define the target. The code starts from a covariate-only table so the selection step cannot accidentally depend on the later stockout outcome.

The redesigned matches balance location and improve the other measured comparisons

Use the original pooled SD and count repeated controls with their weights
Pre-adoption variableRedesigned standardized difference
lead_days0.00
urban0.00
baseline_rate-0.08

Exact location matching makes its mean difference zero. Delivery and baseline rate may remain imbalanced; a value below .10 in absolute magnitude is a common descriptive heuristic, not proof of exchangeability. Inspect overlap, distributions and retained versus excluded profiles too. Do not keep changing the design until an attractive treatment result appears. Remaining imbalance or loss of important adopters can justify requesting more comparison data.

Matching and regression estimate different reductions for the same eighteen retained adopters

The interval belongs to the outcome model, not to the nearest-neighbor contrast
Reduction for retained adoptersPoints
Matching contrast2.67
Regression standardized to these adopters2.98
Regression HC1 interval2.36 to 3.59

Fit the established outcome model to all 50 stores and average its counterfactual design-row contrasts only across the retained adopters. The contrast c gives estimate c′b and SE √(c′Vc). The displayed normal-reference HC1 interval conditions on the observed covariates and the frozen retained target, assumes a suitable outcome mean and independent store errors, and does not incorporate searching over designs or uncertainty about unmeasured causes. It cannot be relabelled as an interval for matching.

Reused controls carry squared weights into uncertainty

Effective control count=(∑jwj)2∑jwj2=8.53Unique controls=10

A control used four times contributes the same outcome four times. Conditional on fixed weights and independent unit outcomes, the variance of a weighted mean contains Σw²Var(Y)/(Σw)²; four appearances contribute sixteen times its individual variance, not four. The effective count shown assumes equal control variances and is a precision diagnostic, not an extra sample size. Full nearest-neighbor inference must account for the estimator and design; treating pairs as independent or automatically bootstrapping their rows is not justified.

Carry a defensible comparison into the management memo

Worked application

The recommendation reports the target, calculation and comparison quality together

  • All-store adjusted reduction: 3.01 points; interval 2.39–3.63
  • Current-adopter model reduction: 3.38 points
  • Matching estimates name their retained adopters
  • The initial propensity attempt fails; inspect the completed redesign above

The management memo should not select one attractive number from a menu of estimators. It should state which stores the number represents and show how their missing comparison was constructed. The next lesson uses a separate rollout cohort and compares changes over time. The general task remains the same: build a credible comparison for the decision population.

Explain, reconstruct, diagnose and transfer

Decision and synthesis

Reusing a control repeats its weight rather than creating independent outcomes

  • Implement exact urban status plus the same logit caliper, then inspect retention and all balance measures before outcomes.
  • A match uses a control four times, so it supplies four independent outcomes. Explain the error and how squared weights affect precision.

Work independently or explain your reasoning to a partner. State the target, units and assumptions before calculating. The student notebook provides runnable setup and separate task cells; the companion solution checks the calculation. The lesson’s completed lab remains available as a reference, with its steps separated into smaller cells.

Stricter matches can improve comparability while narrowing the population represented

  • A stricter design loses the highest-risk adopters. State whose effect remains, which population cannot be covered, and a defensible next step.
  • Submit a calculation, an assumption and a justified next action

An acceptable answer can recommend more information, a narrower claim or no action. It must connect the method to the target and explain the consequence of a failed assumption. Use the assessment criteria after attempting the task; matching a supplied recommendation is not the grading objective.

After your attempt: check the reasoning

Open the assessment criteria

Report retained adopters, unique/reused controls and all three SMDs. Keep targets identical across estimates. The robust regression interval is model-based and conditional on the retained covariates, not a matching interval.

Further reading for the implementation

The score uses the documented inverse penalty setting in scikit-learn LogisticRegression. For why ordinary bootstrap inference can fail for fixed-neighbor matching, see Abadie and Imbens, On the Failure of the Bootstrap for Matching Estimators.

Update the decision memo

For the fifty voluntary-cohort stores, the outcome model estimates a 3.01-point reduction (95% interval 2.39–3.63). The adopter-target estimate is 3.38 points. The propensity matching attempt retains nineteen adopters but worsens urban balance, so its 3.54-point result motivates redesign rather than a separate rollout claim. The location-constrained redesign retains 18 adopters and estimates 2.67 points by matching versus 2.98 by regression for those same adopters. Report its improved measured balance, eight exclusions and reused controls; those checks do not establish absence of unmeasured confounding.

Make the call

The propensity attempt gives 3.54 points. Should the memo compare it with the model’s 3.38-point adopter average and present the larger number as stronger evidence?

Compare your reasoning

First use the model average for the same nineteen retained adopters: 3.03 points. Then inspect comparison quality: the propensity attempt worsens urban balance, so a larger estimated reduction does not make its causal evidence stronger. Revise the comparison using starting variables, then reassess balance and the retained target.

The bigger picture

Regression and matching make the unobserved alternative concrete in different ways. Regression predicts two outcomes for each target profile; matching supplies observed comparisons from other units. In both methods, the credibility of the comparison and the population weights determine what the estimate can contribute to a decision.

After your decision: open the known answer

The known expected reduction for all 50 stores is 3.34 points; for their adopters it is 3.65. Comparing estimates with the matching target separates estimation error from a change in population.
